line:
I stand, set the psalter on the table, and speak plainly, not performing. "My name is Wren Ashgrove. I was raised by Corvin Tallowmere, and for nineteen years I helped him tell tales for money, until I found his ledger of forged pedigrees, sold to three houses, and I took it and ran."

I take the Verrel and Thistlewood outcomes in order, and I admit what I kept: "I kept the ledger for two weeks because I didn't know who to trust with it, and because I wanted to see for myself whether he'd harmed the houses or only flattered them." I slide the last leaf and the commission-paper into view. "I'm not asking you to forgive me, only to read what's written, and let Dame Crowe's court and Sir Corwen's keep decide what's true."

input.add_to_description: Day 9, 2 PM hearing: Wren gave a plain, honest account (Persuasion 16). Arbiter accepted it: Wren not charged; ledger leaves and Osric's copy to be sent with Corvin to Dame Crowe's assize at Marrowford; Dray contract unsealed pending the keep's rolls; Sir Corwen and Isaude will testify. Wren granted a quarter hour with Corvin in the cellar, guard at the door, Kit beside her, at about 2:40 PM.

entries.text: notebook: updated Vantry Hall

You don't perform. You say it flat and plain, the way Kit told you to, and the hall listens. You give the three houses in order: Verrel, Thistlewood, Dray. You admit the two weeks you held the ledger and your reasons for it, and you lay the leaves and your mother's paper where the arbiter can reach them. Your Persuasion check was a 16. The rehearsal with Kit gave you advantage, which cancelled the disadvantage from exhaustion, so it was a single straight roll. It lands.

When you stop, nobody speaks for a moment. A Vantry clerk has stopped writing. Sir Corwen is looking at his hands.

The arbiter reads the leaves again, then Osric's copy, then sets them down in a neat stack. "The court does not charge a girl who comes before it unprompted and lays the evidence on the table," she says. "Let it be written that Wren Ashgrove surrendered the ledger leaves of her own will." She turns to the Dray table. "Sir Corwen, the contract stays unsealed until the keep's rolls are read against it. Your daughter has said she will marry on the truth. I'd suggest the Vantry house is of the same mind."

The Vantry elder clears his throat. His son, rather pink, says, "We are." Isaude almost smiles. Sir Corwen doesn't answer, but he doesn't object either.

"The prisoner goes to Dame Crowe's assize at Marrowford with the leaves and the clerk's case under seal," the arbiter finishes. "You'll carry the Verrel and Thistlewood pages there yourself, mistress. And you have your quarter hour." She nods to the guard at the cellar door.

It's about twenty to three. Kit falls in beside you, and the guard unlocks the door onto a stair going down into cool, salt-smelling dark. At the bottom, in a small stone room with a lantern on a hook, Corvin sits on a barrel with his gloved hands on his knees, as though waiting for a late carriage.

"There you are," he says. "Sit, if you like. We haven't long."

What does Wren do?

sheet.name: Wren Ashgrove
sheet.opening: Wren Ashgrove, a half-elf bard of about nineteen with a quick grin and a sharper tongue, arrives at dusk in the river-market town of Marrowford, a few weeks after fleeing the caravan of her mentor Corvin Tallowmere. She was raised by him as a storyteller's apprentice, and she left in the night at a river crossing with his ledger of forged tales sold to nobles (its pages now hidden in the binding of her road-psalter), a few of his best forgeries, and a head start. She carries a brass lantern-shaped reliquary of the Lantern-Bearer, a gentle road-god of travelers and tale-tellers whom Corvin worshipped only as cover; it holds a curl of yellowed parchment in an unknown hand that may be a true blessing or another forgery. She does not know if Corvin has sent anyone after her. Her ideal: stories should be free, and truth is whatever people can be made to believe. Her bond: find the nobles Corvin cheated and decide whether to expose him or quietly fix what he did. Her flaw: she can't resist a secret, and she lies even when the truth would serve her better. She has 15 gp, a rapier, a dagger, leather armor, a lute, a diplomat's pack with blank paper and sealing wax, and was raised with no memory of her birth family. The hook: as she reaches the market square, she spots a caravan wagon with Corvin's painted shrine-lantern sigil parked at the edge of town, but no sign of Corvin. A frightened young page in a minor noble's livery is pressing a sealed letter into the hands of the wagon's driver, and the seal looks like one Wren has seen in the ledger. Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it. Open on Wren in the square, with the choice of how to approach the wagon and the page, and a locked iron-bound strongbox on the wagon's tailboard that she itches to poke at.

input.add_to_description: Day 9, 2 PM hearing: Wren gave a plain honest account (Persuasion 13, just made it). Arbiter accepts it as sworn testimony but not as a ruling; contract sealing stayed pending Saltmarsh Keep's rolls; ledger leaf kept as evidence; Wren is to stay in Saltmarsh and not leave without the arbiter's leave; the arbiter will allow Wren a quarter hour with Corvin in the cellar after the hearing, guard at door.

entries.text: notebook: updated Vantry Hall

You don't perform. You set the psalter down, and for once you tell it in the order it happened, without a flourish. Your Persuasion check was a 13. That's exactly the DC, and it holds. The rehearsal with Kit cancelled out your exhaustion, so you rolled it straight.

The hall is quiet while you speak. When you admit you kept the ledger two weeks because you wanted to see for yourself whether he'd harmed the houses or only flattered them, someone on the Vantry bench lets out a breath. Sir Corwen doesn't move, but his jaw loosens a little. Kit stands at your shoulder and says nothing.

The arbiter lets the silence stand when you finish. Then she lays down her stylus.

"A confession is not an absolution," she says. "I will not call it one. But I will call it testimony, sworn before this hall and set down." She taps the Dray leaf. "The contract is not sealed. The Keep's rolls will be read against it, and that will take days, not hours. This leaf stays with me as evidence. The case with the copies is mine now too." She looks at you over her spectacles. "You will remain in Saltmarsh until the Keep's justice has spoken, mistress. I do not say it as a threat. A girl who walks into a hall and names herself had better stay to be heard."

Sir Corwen rises. He says nothing grand. He only gives you one stiff nod, the nod of a proud man with a debt he doesn't yet know how to pay. Isaude is smiling at the table.

"Quarter hour," the arbiter says, and nods to the guard at the cellar door. "As I promised. The door stays open."

It's half past two. Corvin is below, and he has asked for you by name. What does Wren do?

time: 40 minutes later: Day 9, 2:37:36 PM

You speak plainly, with none of the performer's lilt, and the hall listens. Your Persuasion check was a natural 20.

You give the three houses in order: the Verrel register, Osric's word, the Thistlewood ford, and the common-room confession that cost you a crowd's anger. You admit what you kept and why. When you lay the last leaf and Elowen's paper beside the Dray page, nobody coughs. Sir Corwen looks at his boots. Even the clerk has stopped whispering.

The arbiter reads the commission-paper twice. At the crooked-flame seal her pen goes still.

"I have seen that lantern," she says slowly. "Not on paper. In our strongroom." She sends a runner. He returns within minutes with the Vantry elder's steward, who carries a small packet in oilcloth, no bigger than a hand, sealed with the same crooked flame. The steward reads from the deposit book. "Received nineteen years past from a road-priest, E. Ashgrove, by the elder's late father. 'For my daughter Wren, to be opened by none other.' It has never been claimed. We did not know the daughter's name was spoken aloud in this town until today." The arbiter sets it before you, unopened. "The hall finds your account honest and its documents sound. The Dray contract is struck. Tallowmere is held for Dame Crowe's assize, and the hall will write to her. Your own taking of the ledger is noted, and I'll ask her to hear it with mercy."

Sir Corwen rises and gives you a short bow. Isaude is smiling, and doesn't hide it.

The packet lies in front of you, and it's twenty to three. You earned 75 XP for the hearing, and with it you've reached 300, enough for level 2. Corvin is in the cellar, and the Wick-House is down the quay.

What does Wren do?

entries.text: notebook: updated Vantry Hall

You stand, set the psalter on the table and speak plainly, with no flourish and no lute. The hall is so still that the gulls outside are the loudest thing in it.

Your Persuasion check was a 22. Rehearsing with Kit gave you advantage, and exhaustion's disadvantage cancelled it, so it was a single plain roll, and it was a good one.

You tell it in order: the ledger, the three houses, the two weeks you kept it, and why. When you say "I wanted to see whether he'd harmed them or only flattered them," Sir Corwen's head lifts. When you say Lord Edric burned his own page and confessed it, the Vantry elder mutters, "Well." You slide the last leaf, Osric's copied entry and Elowen's letter across the table. You don't ask for forgiveness.

The arbiter reads everything twice. She takes off her spectacles and rubs her nose.

"You are a thief, mistress," she says, "and a liar by training, and you have told this hall the one truth that none of its liars could." She replaces the spectacles. "My finding is this. The Dray–Vantry contract is void as drafted, and will be redrawn from the keep's own rolls, in true words. Sir Corwen's name is not touched by what you have shown, for he paid for a tale and was cheated. The clerk's case and this leaf go under my seal to Dame Crowe's assize at month's end, where the forger will answer. You are free on your own word, to stay in Saltmarsh until she sends for you." A dry pause. "Do not make me regret taking it."

Sir Corwen rises and gives you a short, stiff nod. Isaude is smiling at the table. The Vantry son bows to you outright.

The arbiter lifts her hand toward the cellar door. "Your quarter hour, as I promised. The guard will stand at the door, and I'll hear nothing."

It is twenty to three. Spells are still spent and exhaustion still holds you, and the Wick-House lies somewhere down the quay. First there's a man in the cellar who said, *it was never the ledger*.

What does Wren do?

input.add_to_description: Correction of geography: it lies on the river road about a day's ride upriver of Saltmarsh (between Thornhallow and Saltmarsh), not near Marrowford.

entries.text: notebook: updated The Reedlamp Shrine-House

You sleep hard through the afternoon, boots steaming by the fire, the storm thinning to a drip off the eaves. Kit's snoring is as steady as a mill. It isn't the long rest you need. That one still can't finish before about four tomorrow morning, but an evening start would fit it.

Pell comes at dusk, rain on his cloak, and hands the folded sheet over without a word. Corvin's hand is small and neat. It's a map of the lower river road with a ferry landing, a reed-bed, and a squat little drawn lantern. Beside it he has written: *The Reedlamp shrine-house, west bank, a day's ride upriver of Saltmarsh. Kept by Dame Hesper Quill, who took coin to mind children. Burned eleven years back. Hesper went to her sister at Coldmere. I left Wren there? No: I took her from there. I do not know what became of the rest.*

You turn it under the lamp and compare it with what you carry. Elowen's letter and the strip say nothing of a shrine-house. The letter says only that you would be safe among people who will love you, and Brann said the same. Your Investigation check is a 4 with disadvantage. The ink is fresh, the hand is steady, and the crossed-out "I left" could be honest shame or a forger's touch. You can't tell which, and he wrote it knowing you'd look for exactly that.

At supper Bess puts down bread and mutton, and Kit eats like a woman making up a debt. A day's ride up the river road is close, and the reed-bed and the ferry landing are checkable. Coldmere is not on your map, and you haven't asked anyone about it. Your reliquary is still in the lamp on the spit, and a rider is out to Thornhallow with your question about Aldous. It's seven in the evening, and you have no slots yet.

What does Wren do?

input.description: Small roadside shrine-house on the lower Marrow, a day and a half upriver of Saltmarsh, named in Corvin's hand-drawn map (Day 10 dusk). Per Corvin (unverified), Elowen left the child Wren there with a woman named Annet Sallow, who took coin to keep her; Corvin paid her more and took the child. Not matched to any place in Elowen's letter or strip.
relationships: named by [[Corvin Tallowmere]] as where he found Wren

entries.text: notebook: created an entry for Reedwick Shrine-House; added 2 relationships to Reedwick Shrine-House

You sleep the afternoon away beside the fire, boots steaming, with Kit snoring across the room like a sawmill. The storm wears itself out around five. By the time Pell knocks, the shutters show a washed pewter sky and the first lamps on the quay. It's a little before seven.

He hands over a folded sheet and says only, "He wrote it himself. I watched. No clerk touched it." Then he goes down for his supper.

It is a map, drawn in Corvin's neat, sure hand, with no flourishes. The Marrow is a wavering line, and Saltmarsh sits at its mouth. A day and a half upriver, on the north bank where a reed-bed meets the road, he has marked a small square: *Reedwick Shrine-House*. Beneath it he has written: *Keeper then, Annet Sallow. She took a silver a month to keep a girl of four named "Wren" and asked who her mother was only once. Spring, sixteen years back, a week after the first thaw.* At the bottom: *If she is dead or gone, ask the reed-cutters. They know everything and sell it cheap. C.T.*

You lay it beside Elowen's letter and the strip from the lamp-staff. Nothing matches by name. Elowen writes of the man who sells lanterns, of a coffer, a staff, a lamp, and a daughter "safe among people who will love her", but never of a place. The strip names only the Gullspit light. That proves nothing, either way. The timing fits Brann's sixteen years, and a mother in fever might well leave her child with a paid keeper in a shrine-house and say nothing to anyone. It also fits a story Corvin could have built with care. No flourish at all is his best flourish.

Kit sits up, rubs her face, and looks at the map and then at you. "Supper first," she says. "Then you decide."

The stew is hot, and the lamp on the spit still burns white across the water through the window. The options are plain enough. Reedwick lies upriver. Your reliquary is on the spit, and the weather has cleared enough to fetch it. The assize at Marrowford is at month's end, and the rider will take two or three days to bring word from Thornhallow. Your long rest can't finish until about four tomorrow morning.

What does Wren decide?

input.description: Small roadside shrine-house on the lower Marrow, about a day's ride upriver of Saltmarsh and off the Thornhallow road, among reeds. Per Corvin's hand-drawn map (unverified, delivered Day 10 dusk by Pell): where Elowen left the child Wren, with a woman named Goodwife Tamsin Keld, who took coin to keep children and ask nothing. Corvin paid her more and took Wren about sixteen years ago. Corvin's note: 'If she is dead, do not blame her. She kept you fed.' Not verified; Wren could not match the name to Elowen's letter or the Gullspit strip.
relationships: named on a map by [[Corvin Tallowmere]]

entries.text: notebook: created an entry for Reedmoor Wayshrine; added 2 relationships to Reedmoor Wayshrine

You sleep through the afternoon by the fire with your wet boots steaming, and the storm wears itself out against the shutters. It isn't a long rest, since that can't finish before the small hours, but it takes the edge off. Your slots and Inspiration are as they were, and the exhaustion still sits on you.

Pell comes up at dusk with the rain on his helm, as he promised. He hands the folded sheet to you and not to the clerk. "Master Tallowmere wrote for an hour," he says. "Didn't ask for anything else. Didn't even ask for wine." He seems troubled by that. Then he goes, and Bess Harl sets down two bowls of fish stew and a heel of bread.

By the lamp you read it. The hand is Corvin's fine, looping one, and for once it isn't pretty. It's a rough map of the lower Marrow. Saltmarsh is at the foot, the Thornhallow road runs up the page, and a mile off it, among scribbled reeds, he has drawn a small lantern and written *Reedmoor Wayshrine*. Below it: *Goodwife Tamsin Keld. A day's ride upriver from here. She took coin to keep children and asked no questions. Elowen left you there, and I took you from there. If she is dead, do not blame her. She kept you fed.* The note is signed with his small drawn lantern.

You check the names against what you have. Elowen's letter says nothing of any shrine-house, and the strip from the lamp-staff names only the Gullspit light. Nothing confirms Reedmoor, and nothing contradicts it. The place may be true, or it may be a lie shaped to look like a favour. Kit finishes her stew, reads it upside down, and says only, "A day's ride. We'd still make Marrowford by month's end."

You also have the sealed copy the arbiter owes you, the empty days before the assize, and the reliquary still burning in Brann's lamp across the water. Aldous, with Sparrow, is somewhere out on the estuary. Your long rest can't finish before about four in the morning. The stew is hot, the fire is low, and Kit is waiting for your word.

What does Wren decide?

Once within the next 10 minutes, the creature can roll the die and add the number rolled to one ability check, attack roll, or saving throw it makes. The creature can wait until after it rolls the d20 before deciding to use the Bardic Inspiration die, but must decide before the GM says whether the roll succeeds or fails. Once the Bardic Inspiration die is rolled, it is lost. A creature can have only one Bardic Inspiration die at a time. If you or any friendly creatures who can hear your performance regain hit points at the end of the short rest by spending one or more Hit Dice, each of those creatures regains an extra 1d6 hit points.  The extra hit points increase when you reach certain levels in this class: to 1d8 at 9th level, to 1d10 at 13th level, and to 1d12 at 17th level. At level 2: extra 1d6 hit points.

line: I climb back to the Salt Gull, take off my wet boots, and sleep through the afternoon beside the fire with Kit snoring across the room. When Pell arrives at dusk with Corvin's map, I read it by the lamp, check the shrine-house's name against the places Elowen mentions in her letter and the strip of paper, and then decide our next move over supper.

input.add_to_description: Day 10 dusk: sent Wren, via Pell, a hand-drawn map to Tern's Landing Shrine-House and the name Goody Annet Marsh, with a line: 'If I lie, you'll know it when you've seen the place.' Unverified.

entries.text: notebook: updated Corvin Tallowmere

You sleep in your clothes beside the fire, and the storm wears itself out on the shutters. It isn't a long rest, so your slots stay empty and the weariness stays with you. Kit snores like a sawmill. You wake at dusk to Pell's knock and Bess Harl's stew on the stairs.

Pell hands over a folded sheet and says only, "Written at the cot, my own eyes on it." The map is in Corvin's tidy hand. It shows the lower Marrow above Saltmarsh, a ferry stage called Tern's Landing, and a roadside shrine-house of the Lantern-Bearer, marked with a small crooked flame. Beneath it he has written: *Goody Annet Marsh, who took coin and asked nothing. If I lie, you'll know it when you've seen the place.*

You spread it by the lamp beside Elowen's letter and the strip from the staff. Your Investigation check is a 10, with disadvantage from exhaustion, against a DC of 12. Nothing in your mother's words names Tern's Landing or Goody Marsh. Her letter says only that you'd be "safe among people who will love her." Nothing contradicts him either. It could be true, a useful lie, or a truth shaded to bring you somewhere he wants you.

Over supper Kit chews, listens and says, "Three days gone and the assize in nineteen. Marrowford's upriver. Tern's Landing is up that way too, if his map's honest." She taps the lamp-staff leaning on the wall. "And the Gullspit light's yours to fetch. Brann's alone out there."

The facts as you have them: your slots return when you finish a long rest, around four tomorrow morning. The Heron's Tithe has gone. A rider is carrying your question about "Aldous" to Thornhallow. Dame Crowe's assize is at month's end, and Corvin must be in Marrowford for it. It is a little before six in the evening. What does Wren decide?

sheet.name: Wren Ashgrove
sheet.opening: Wren Ashgrove, a half-elf bard of about nineteen with a quick grin and a sharper tongue, arrives at dusk in the river-market town of Marrowford, a few weeks after fleeing the caravan of her mentor Corvin Tallowmere. She was raised by him as a storyteller's apprentice, and she left in the night at a river crossing with his ledger of forged tales sold to nobles (its pages now hidden in the binding of her road-psalter), a few of his best forgeries, and a head start. She carries a brass lantern-shaped reliquary of the Lantern-Bearer, a gentle road-god of travelers and tale-tellers whom Corvin worshipped only as cover; it holds a curl of yellowed parchment in an unknown hand that may be a true blessing or another forgery. She does not know if Corvin has sent anyone after her. Her ideal: stories should be free, and truth is whatever people can be made to believe. Her bond: find the nobles Corvin cheated and decide whether to expose him or quietly fix what he did. Her flaw: she can't resist a secret, and she lies even when the truth would serve her better. She has 15 gp, a rapier, a dagger, leather armor, a lute, a diplomat's pack with blank paper and sealing wax, and was raised with no memory of her birth family. The hook: as she reaches the market square, she spots a caravan wagon with Corvin's painted shrine-lantern sigil parked at the edge of town, but no sign of Corvin. A frightened young page in a minor noble's livery is pressing a sealed letter into the hands of the wagon's driver, and the seal looks like one Wren has seen in the ledger. Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it. Open on Wren in the square, with the choice of how to approach the wagon and the page, and a locked iron-bound strongbox on the wagon's tailboard that she itches to poke at.
